text.en: The Rav argues that the very fact that the other major religions must accept Toras Moshe, and can only claim it was altered, testifies to its truth, because of the unique event at Sinai.
Shemitah's promise of a crop for three years is a promise only Hashem can make; a human founder could not make it, and that is why such founders removed the difficult mitzvos.
A small detail, like a story about Alexander's horse missing a tooth, can be invented by one writer, but the core of an event that multitudes lived through cannot.
The halachah that one extra or missing letter makes a Sefer Torah invalid is a built-in protection against change, which is why Sifrei Torah of long-separated communities match letter for letter.
The nations' hatred of the Jews comes from jealousy: deep down they know the greatness of the Jewish people.

Giving something while knowing one will take it back is not called changing one's mind but not giving at all; since Hashem knows the future, the claim that He changed His mind about the Torah makes Him a liar.

The Rav reverses the usual mark of a great work: a man-made masterpiece is finished once grasped, while the Torah, like a schoolbook that is never outgrown, is used by the child of nine and the gedolim alike, and this very inexhaustibility is a proof of its Divine origin.
The endlessness of the Torah and the endlessness of nature have the same cause: both are made by Hashem, so neither can be sealed off as finished.

The Torah proves itself through predictions that could have failed: it promised that Yehoshua would cross the Jordan and conquer, though he could have fallen sick or died in battle, and it told the tribes their portions in advance, yet required a lottery that came out exactly so.
The Rav calls the existence of the Jewish people in exile a greater wonder than the Exodus, the splitting of the sea and the miracles in the wilderness, only one that people take for granted.

The cultures of Egypt, Rome and Greece are studied today by a handful of professors, while the Torah is alive among hundreds of thousands who learn it daily, not as an academic course; this contrast fulfills the promise that the Torah will not be forgotten.

Emunas tzaddikim is part of emunah itself: the Torah describes the height of emunah at the sea as belief in Hashem and in Moshe His servant, and the Rav adds that one must also believe in oneself, since all Jews are tzaddikim.

Because Hashem looked into the Torah to create the world, anything that exists in the world must be found in the Torah; a tzaddik's knowledge of medicine or of the future is drawn from the Torah, not from outside study.

The Torah's daring promise that no one will covet a Jew's land while he goes up to Yerushalayim with his whole family is something no human author could have written; it shows the Torah's divine source.
Details reported by a single historian may be doubted, but the bare existence of a figure witnessed by multitudes cannot; this is the type of certainty on which Matan Torah rests.

The worldwide identity of the Sefer Torah is itself a proof: Jews separated for centuries by geography, with no means of contact, are found to hold the same text letter for letter, preserved by the halachah that one missing letter disqualifies a Sefer Torah.
The Rav explains that Moshe Rabbeinu's miracles in the midbar were not done to prove anything; each was done because it was needed, such as drowning the Mitzrim or the earth swallowing the rebels.
Since every Jew heard Hashem appoint Moshe, the nevuah of Moshe is for us as clear as daylight, so no wonder can compete with it; the question is never who shows bigger miracles.
Obeying any later navi is itself a mitzvah from Moshe Rabbeinu's Torah, like obeying witnesses, and not a matter of being convinced by his miracles.
The Rav answers Rashi's question by explaining that milah and gid hanasheh are known only because Moshe told us of them, so HaChodesh hazeh lachem is the first mitzvah heard from Moshe Rabbeinu.

He reads 'Moshe av lanevi'im' as meaning that even the nevi'im before Moshe, like Avraham and Yaakov, are known through him, and those after him are believed because he commanded us to listen to them.
Just as every force of holiness has its opposite, emunah above the intellect is matched by a kefirah above the intellect: refusing to believe what the intellect itself sees.
What the Jews saw at the sea was knowledge, not belief, like seeing daylight through an open window; their emunah was in what lay beyond that, what Moshe Rabbeinu told them of heaven.
Amalek is listed among the chiefs of Edom who trembled at the splitting of the sea, so his attack weeks later was a denial of what he himself had seen, the exact reverse of Jewish emunah.
The other religions are not a denial of the Torah but a rationalization: unable to keep it, they claim that Hashem changed His mind.
Hashem cannot be said to change His mind, since He already knows what will be later; this is why the Torah's own promise that it will never change is decisive.
The Mishnah names its Tannaim not only to know who said what: a tzaddik who learns lishmah becomes so holy that his very name is Torah, so saying 'Rabbi Akiva' is like saying a word of Torah.

A name in loshon hakodesh is the creature's essence: Adam saw from each animal's nature which letters it was made of, and a sinner loses his name, which is why Zimri and Cozbi are named only after Pinchas killed them.
The holier a thing is, the more easily it is spoiled; wine, which stands for the reward of Olam Haba, is spoiled even by a gentile's look, showing how holy that reward is.
World events like Vashti's death or Nixon's resignation are reported with worldly reasons, but their true cause is the tzaddikim and Klal Yisrael, which will become clear only when Moshiach comes.
The heavenly calls to teshuvah go out every day, and the receiver that picks them up is a Jewish heart; a sudden urge to do teshuvah is the heart catching one of them.
Machlokes comes from each person's private interests; one who learns lishmah has none, which is why he can love everyone, as all will in the days of Moshiach.
Loving a fellow Jew does not divide one's love of Hashem, since every Jew's neshamah is a part of Hashem; this is why 'love your fellow as yourself' ends with 'I am Hashem'.
The Rav reads 'baruch shebachar bahem uvemishnasam' not only as praise of Hashem but as praise of the talmid who chose to devote his life to these Chachamim and their Torah.
The halachic fact that saying a Chacham's name is not a hefsek in learning Torah shows that his name itself has become Torah.
The oversized fruit of Eretz Yisrael in the meraglim's time came from the abnormal amount of Torah being learned in the Midbar, since every good word builds and blesses the world.

Unlike an English word such as 'lion', which is only an agreed label, the Hebrew name aryeh is made of the very letters that give the lion its existence and character; a Tanna's name likewise is the substance of his neshamah.
Saying 'Rabbi Meir' before his halacha is more than honor: it draws part of his neshamah into the learner, just as Moshe Rabbeinu was endowed with the power of a holy name when he said it.
The more holy something is, the more easily it is spoiled, as with levels of tumah and with wine; this is why the Olam Haba of one who learns Torah lishmah may not be seen at all.

The Chasam Sofer reads 'and this shira shall answer before it' as the remedy for troubles that contradict each other: when any prayer for one trouble worsens the other, Torah protects without taking a side.
Praying for peace is itself a problem in wartime, since the war may be the beginning of the geulah; this is what makes war a bee-and-scorpion trouble.
Achashverosh rising to power outside the normal rules shows Hashem's hand in appointing him, and the Rav sees the same in Bush becoming president with fewer popular votes.
The forcing of the Torah at Sinai is like the involuntary muscles of the heart and lungs: what life depends on is not left to a person's will.
Chizkiyahu's calm sleep on the night Sancheirev was destroyed is read into the passuk of singing on their beds: the Jews fight with their mouth, not with missiles.

Shirah means harmony: beings who are not at peace in their feelings cannot sing together, so the malachim's love for each other is what makes their song possible, and the Yidden who sang at the sea in their place needed that same love.
Hashem creates only what He likes, so nothing in the world lacks a reason to be loved; if Hashem appreciates it, a person should too.
The king who begged two devoted friends to take him into their friendship illustrates that where friends love each other as themselves, Hashem wants to be there too.
Anavah is described as a garment: it can be put on and taken off, since a leader sometimes has to show authority, and knowing when and how much takes da'as of kedushah.
A pancake that squirted hot fat into a tzaddik's face in the middle of learning was itself the sign that it was treif: such brazenness could not come from kosher food.
The yetzer hara enters the batei midrash disguised as 'Yesh', so that learning turns into a source of ego instead of anavah.
The four animals with one kosher sign symbolize the worst exiles precisely because a good feature used for evil makes something worse, and so learning without menschlichkeit makes a person worse.
Hachodesh hazeh lachem is the first mitzvah only retroactively: once Hashem at Har Sinai commanded belief in all that Moshe says, it became the first mitzvah received through Moshe.
Even the mitzvos of the Avos and the stories of Bereishis are not believed on the authority of the Avos or of historical records, but only because Moshe, appointed at Sinai, wrote them.

The Rav compares the obligation to heed a navi to the obligation to accept two witnesses: in both, belief rests on Hashem's command, not on the person's feats, while belief in Sinai itself rests on fact.
The other religions' acceptance of Matan Torah, and their fight over Yerushalayim, are themselves evidence that the Jewish mesorah cannot be refuted.
Something first carries the quality of reishis, like the head from which every action of the body comes; that is why Rashi expects the Torah's opening to be the first mitzvah.
Kiddush HaChodesh belongs to Eretz Yisrael because it was the first land created, yet a greater chacham abroad may declare the month, since the neshamah outweighs geography.
Jews count every day as part of the new month, even the thirtieth, when the moon is dark: a Jew is always within renewal.
Rebbi's refusal to curse a king dead for centuries shows that learning a passage is not reading history: the learner is lifted into that era, where Nebuchadnezzar is still a living king.
Like the Aron that took no space, Torah came from heaven where measurement does not apply, and so it carries the learner beyond space and time.

Lechem is three times the simple Shem Havayah while matzah is three times its milui, the same value as adam, so the passuk that man lives not by bread alone points to a higher level reached through matzah.
Sefer Bereishis is Torah too sublime to be reduced to halachos about physical objects; its 'objects' are the Avos themselves, which is why it is learned by accompanying them.
The Torah leaves out Moshe's parents at his birth and Avraham's righteousness at his calling to teach that the Jewish people did not come by merit or chance but because creation itself required them.
The Ramban, who knew the Zohar's answers, deliberately opens Avraham's story with his faults so no one would think he was chosen for his tzidkus.
Inverting the Reishis Chochmah's image, the Rav says it is not Gehinom but this world that lies in the street, while its true Master is hidden, which is exactly why the word olam means concealment.

The heretic who would laugh at anyone saying his house built itself still claims that of the whole world; the Rav explains he must invent a theory of origins only because he refuses to believe the Chumash.

Moshe's blessing to Levi can be checked against reality: of ten roshei yeshiva in Torah Vodaath seven were kohanim or levi'im, and most of the classic commentators around the Shulchan Aruch were too, a sign of Hashem visible in the Torah world.

The Rav distinguishes two lines among the leaders of Klal Yisrael: the moreh hora'ah of Shevet Levi, and the Chassidishe Rebbes, like the Ba'al HaTanya, who descend from David HaMelech and carry malchus.
That the same Chumash and Gemara serve a person for his whole life, with new insights at every stage, is itself a proof that the Torah is from Heaven, since no human textbook behaves this way.
Heresy has nothing to do with science: a baker or a candlestick maker can be just as much a kofer, but no one puts a microphone in front of the baker.

The Rav presents the absence of open revelations in this generation as its particular test: believing without seeing is a great tikun, and through it this generation can accomplish more than earlier ones and bring the days of Moshiach.

The proof is in what the books do not need: a textbook is discarded once outgrown, but a Chumash is never obsolete, and the very same Gemara is learned by a nine-year-old and by the greatest roshei yeshiva.
The Rav argues that no human being could compose a wisdom that is plain to a child and endlessly deep to a genius, so the Torah's endless depth is itself a wonder testifying to its divine origin.
A Torah sefer from the Infinite has no bottom, while digging into a secular book only makes a hole in the page: its wisdom goes no deeper than the paper.
The Rav reads the Greeks' failure to defile the one sealed jar as a matter of sight: they looked at it again and again and did not see it, because they were not given permission to see it.

Avraham Avinu's discovery of Hashem through the order of the world is presented as a path for everyone: whoever strengthens his emunah will reach a point where Hashem shows him 'I am here' through wonders in his Torah and his daily life.
Emunah, being a mitzvah, has halachos like a sukkah: the instinctive, natural and philosophical paths to faith are not its halachic definition.
The Rambam in the Yad speaks of emunah as halacha, differently from his philosophical approach in the Moreh Nevuchim.
Even other religions accept the Torah because a public revelation cannot be denied; they can only claim it was later replaced.
Moshe's wonders, such as the splitting of the sea and the mann, were done because they were needed, not as proofs that he was right.
Belief in a navi works like belief in witnesses: not certainty about the person, but trust in Hashem's command, for Hashem stands among the judges.
Belief in any prophet but Moshe is only a decree, like trusting two witnesses who could be lying; true knowledge of Hashem belongs to Klal Yisroel alone through what they saw at Sinai.
The verse 'Hashem is not a man that He should lie or change His mind' was said by Bilaam, a gentile, so the nations' own prophet testifies against the idea of a new testament.
Rashi's statement that HaChodesh is the first mitzvah Yisroel were commanded is simple according to the Rambam: it is the first mitzvah received from Moshe, the only prophet believed with certainty.
The Rambam's words that Moshe is 'father to the prophets before him' mean that even the Avos and Adam are believed only because Moshe recorded their mitzvos.
A Jew who kept the Torah all his life never recants at death, while sinners often repent then, because at death rationalization falls away and only the truth remains.
The Rav rests the truth of the Torah not on miracles a person must take on trust but on a public event: millions heard Hashem speak at once, and an event seen by so many cannot be denied.
He reads the mitzvah that every Jew write a sefer Torah as a test of truth: the identical Torah given to everyone described events the whole generation had seen itself, so it could be checked by all.
He points out that those who received the sefer Torah had been children under twenty in the wilderness and were now grown men who remembered everything that had happened.
He argues that a teaching that lets people eat whatever they want would be easily accepted, so the acceptance of a Torah full of hard obligations itself shows its truth.

The Torah opens with Bereishis, creation in thought (Tishrei), rather than with the month of action (Nissan), to show that what is first in thought is primary; so Israel, though created later, is 'reishis' and has the true claim to the land.
Hashem deliberately gave the Torah's measures through fruits whose size cannot be fixed, so that no Jew could manage without a talmid chacham.

Bikkurim served a halachic purpose: the kohen in Yerushalayim who saw the seven species from all over the land each year could rule on that year's shiurim, which explains 'the kohen of those days', the yearly blessing, and the restriction to the seven species.

One can stand on the soil of Eretz Yisrael, even on Har HaBayis, and not be in Eretz Yisrael, just as one can be in the day of Shabbos without being in Shabbos; the bikkurim declaration, recalling the Exodus, proclaims that the bringer has left the land of the nations.
Eretz Yisrael is to space what Rosh Hashanah is to the year, and the forty days from Elul to Yom Kippur are Eretz Yisrael in time, which is why Ki Savo is read then.
The statement that a ben sorer umoreh never was and never will be teaches that no Jew can be given up on as lost; whoever looks like the worst can become the best.
Ki Savo's curses end without consolation because they themselves are concealed blessings, and the work of Elul is to uncover them.

The leaves grow first but the tree was planted for the fruit; so too the world was created in thought in Tishrei but in deed in Nisan, and the Torah opens with Bereishis to show that what is first in thought, Israel and the talmid chacham, is the primary thing.
The Torah deliberately left its shiurim unclear so that a Jew would never be able to manage alone and would always need to ask a talmid chacham.
The purpose of bringing bikkurim to the kohen was to learn halachah: from the seven species brought from every region, the kohen could fix that year's shiurim, which changed with Israel's merits.
A gentile in Eretz Yisrael walks on a strip of foreign land; likewise a Jew can live in the Land, or stand in Shabbos or in Elul, without being in it, unless he connects to it.
Since the purpose is learning, the kohen of one's own days is essential; today the 'kohen' to whom one brings bikkurim can be a rebbe, a friend, or the author of a sefer.
The ben sorer umoreh teaches that no Jew is ever lost: the one that Tanna saw later became such a tzaddik that people sat at his grave.

The Rav explains Chizkiyahu's sword through the laws of war: since Torah was the actual weapon against Sancheiriv, one who left the beis medrash was a deserter, subject to the treatment of a fleeing soldier.
Learning differs from davening: in davening a person speaks to Hashem, while in learning Hashem speaks through the person's own mouth.
The Rav cites a saying that the word Gemara relates to burning coals, so it must be learned with fire.
Amalek before Purim and chametz after Purim are the same enemy under another name, the yetzer hara, which explains the extraordinary strictness of the laws of chametz.
The two commands to erase Amalek correspond to Amalek's body, which is killed physically, and its soul, the yetzer hara, which must be nullified.

A lack of desire to learn is like a lack of appetite: a symptom of a deeper cause, so incentives that only push a person to learn miss the point, just as a doctor would not simply tell such a patient to eat.
The words of Torah are like the gold case of a costly watch: the case does not show the value, which lies in the inner works; so too the knowledge of a sugya is only a vessel for the light within it.
Even a Gemara about a thief's claims carries the light of Torah, so the difference between Torah and science is not the subject matter but whether the light comes down through the learner.
Reb Aharon of Karlin's saying: mikvah is not a mitzvah, yet what it brings no mitzvah can bring, because when one purifies himself holiness comes running to him, and then learning and davening go.
Speaking about negel vasser, mikvah and a clean body is not speaking about side matters but about Torah itself, since they are its preparation.
Since a name expresses the soul, and the soul of one who learns lishmah becomes one with the Torah, the very names of the chachamim in the baraisa are Torah.
Like meat placed in the middle of a fire that itself becomes fire, a talmid chacham's soul becomes Torah itself.
The announcement of dawn in the Beis Hamikdash mentioned Chevron in order to recall the Avos, showing that merely mentioning a holy name draws down salvation.
'Mishnah' means doubling: a tzaddik's words to a person carry a second address to Hashem, which is why David's blessings to Naval were not flattery.
The same Torah takes on the color of each receiver's middah, like water poured into glasses of different colors.
Refinement brings sensitivity: wine, used for Kiddush and likened to Olam Haba, is affected even by a goy's touch, and Olam Haba is so delicate that even a glance affects it.

The Oral Torah is 'written' on the heart and mouth of the Jew who learns properly, a private code between Hashem and His people; therefore even when its words are available in translation, it is not truly Oral Torah for the nations.
'From Sinai' means 'because of Sinai': as Hashem chose the lowest mountain, Moshe reasoned that he, who saw himself as the lowest man, was the one obligated to receive the Torah.

The prophets speak for Hashem, the chassan, so they could not praise Him with what was not seen; the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah speak for Knesses Yisroel, the kallah, who sees the survival of the lamb among the wolves as His might, and so they restored the praise.
The Mishnah says Moshe 'received' rather than that Hashem 'gave over', because no human can take over the infinite Torah entirely; but Moshe did give all of it over to Yehoshua.
The last words of the Torah allude to the broken luchos, and the last generations before Moshiach are those broken luchos; yet broken luchos were also kept in the aron.
Today's 'might and awe' of Hashem is the Jew who still manages to say words of tefillah and Torah while the wolves of the yetzer hara tear at his mouth.

The three directives of the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah answer three ways the Torah weakens over the generations: deliberation in judgment for lost knowledge and siyata diShmaya, many students for fewer learners, and a fence for weakened yiras Shamayim.

Torah is a 'small that holds the many' even in a physical sense: the same printed Chumash or Gemara serves a five-year-old and the greatest gedolim, who need no other book because they see more in the same words.

Rabbi Akiva's teachings were beyond Moshe Rabbeinu not from Moshe's lack but because the tagim, the crowns attached to the letters, come from a higher world, as converts attached to Klal Yisroel can reach higher things.

Learning the parsha of the korbanos earns the reward of the large korban: 'zos toras hayoledes' is written by the rich woman's korban, not the poor one's, because through Torah anyone can reach the greatest level.

In the future, the nations' claim that they built roads for Yisroel will be shown false and true at once: they built for themselves, yet in truth everything they made existed only so that Jews could serve Hashem.

Normally aleph signals curse and beis blessing, but where Torah begins, with the aleph of 'Anochi', the aleph is even higher than the beis, as pepper's sharpness gives food more taste than sweetness alone.
The Mishnah lists 'rei'a' and 'ohev' without saying to whom, because Torah unites Hashem and the Jewish soul so fully that there is no separate address to name.
Loving a Jew does not divide one's love of Hashem, since one loves the Jew for his G-dly portion; therefore love of Hashem can be measured by love of Yisroel.
The Rav reads 'malbishto anavah' precisely: true humility is too lofty for a physical person to own in essence, so Torah gives it to him as a garment he wears.
A person's possessions are an extension of his soul, so the holiness of one who learns lishmah spreads even to his animal, which is why Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey refused untithed food.

Torah is the eighth verse of Tehillim 19 after seven verses on nature, and the eighth corresponds to a world above the seven days of creation; Tehillim 119 goes through the alef-beis eight times for the same reason.
Through Sha'arei Orah the Rav links yovel, Binah, geulah, Yom Kippur, the shofar, milah and neder as names of one level above nature, so each of them can free a person from the 'nets' of this world.

The Ramban's distinction between 'by Hashem' and 'to Hashem' becomes a key: a shevuah binds a person through the G-dliness present in this world, while a neder ties him to Binah above it, which is why a neder helps where tefillah, which comes from malchus, cannot.

The custom of checking tzitzis each morning is explained not as a technical precaution but as preparation for the battle of tefillah: through their eight threads one connects to the eighth world before davening.
From the Ba'al HaTanya's arrangement the Rav learns that the aim is not only for each person to finish his own masechta: in a group completing Shas, each one is linked to the entire Shas.
Completing the whole Shas is beyond anyone's grasp, as is even one halachah; yet through the bond of souls in the group, a person who learned a small part is counted as having finished it all.
The Rav reads the Midrash's 'sixty are the queens' as teaching that learning a masechta is a form of malchus, and that even one who learns halachah after halachah is connected to this malchus.
Malchus here means that a Jew has a say in Heaven, and this is what Jews need at a time like this.
When Jews in Eretz Yisroel and abroad each learn and daven for the other, their tefillos join, since all tefillah goes up through Eretz Yisroel and Yerushalayim.

The Rav contrasts the Nefesh HaChaim's lishmah, learning in order to know what the Torah says, with the Tanya's lishmah, binding the soul to the G-dliness in the Torah, and says these are different levels.
Nowadays a person holds sparks of many souls, so after a few years his desire moves from one area of learning to another, as he finishes repairing one part of his soul and moves to the next.
The 'secret' of every Jew is a grace he holds before Hashem that no other Jew has and that he himself cannot name; if he thinks he has found it, that is a sign he has not.
The passuk calls Pinchas 'son of Elazar son of Aharon HaKohen' a second time because once the souls of Nadav and Avihu entered him, he became also a son of Aharon himself.

The people who were tamei were people who had dealt with Nadav and Avihu and received a spark of their souls; that spark of the inner Torah made them feel that tumah could not separate them from all other Jews.
Learning not lishmah leads to lishmah because the angels see only the outside, while Hashem sees the hidden point in the Jew that learns lishmah even then.

Speech of Torah is breath, which has almost no substance but surrounds the whole body, so learning Torah is a garment over all of a person, like tzitzis and sukkah and unlike mitzvos tied to one limb.
Torah learned with love and awe does what the passing of tzaddikim otherwise does: it lifts the judgments to their root in Binah and sweetens them there.

Rashi joins Mordechai and Esther in one explanation because both sought to die as an atonement, and 'what came upon them' is the next verse, 'kiymu v'kiblu': their self-sacrifice brought Torah with love, so the sacrifice itself was no longer needed.
Following the Chasam Sofer, an early improvement can be a trick of the Satan to weaken prayer while the decree still stands, which is why Mordechai returned to his sackcloth and fasting.
Amalek attacked just as the Jews were climbing toward Sinai, because their desire for Torah had weakened; Haman, his descendant, rose under the same conditions, when the Jews were lax in mitzvos.
The souls of a beis medrash's chevra are bound together from above, corresponding to a chevra on high, so the people who come together to one beis medrash are not there by chance.
Just as Ezra had to separate the people from foreign wives before the Second Temple, mass intermarriage today precedes the Third, since everything written in Tanach is eternal.
In the Satmar Rav's story, what troubled the tzaddik was not the missed custom itself but that he had become worse, and the Rav says a person must likewise ask why he has cooled off.
